extracted_by: hand, T-0312 — the Democrat read, March 1834
note: Vol. I No. 16, and there is no No. 15½: the deposit supplies no issue for 11 March and the transcription of this one says so on its own face — 'No March 11 issue is supplied; the printed sequence resumes with March 18, No. 16.' The issue's own contribution is public rather than commercial: a court house in the town of Chicago, named in an attachment notice; the Eagle Hotel, named as the room a county meeting will sit in; an estray of four head described ear by ear out of the county clerk's estray book; the mails' whole weekly rhythm over the postmaster's signature; and the Prices Current's building-materials block, which is what brick, shingles, poplar and stone cost in Chicago that week. Beside them, the standing advertisements of 4 March run on, and two of them — W. Kimball's corner and J. Allen's poplar specification — are legible here where the earlier crop had crushed them.

claims.notes: THE EAGLE HOTEL, CHICAGO — a named hotel, and the first this corpus records. It is named as the place a county political meeting will be held at two in the afternoon, which tells a reconstruction something specific about the building: it has a room that will take a public meeting, so it is not a two-room tavern. Chicago's public rooms as this month documents them are now Dexter Graves's house (where the Board of Trustees sat on 5 March), the Presbyterian and Baptist meeting houses, the Infant School House, School District No. 1's school house, the court house, and this. NO POSITION IS GIVEN and none is inferred. THE DATE MOVES: this notice sets the meeting for 12 April, and the same notice reprinted on 1834-03-25 sets it for the 16th (claim c012 there). Both are recorded as printed; which stood is not stated by either.

claims.notes: A COURT HOUSE IN THE TOWN OF CHICAGO, stated as a fact of procedure rather than announced: the May term of the Cook Circuit Court is 'to be holden at the court house in the town of Chicago' on 14 May 1834. That is the town's first documented court house in this corpus, and it is a public building of a kind the reconstruction does not yet carry. The clerk's office is a separate room again — it moved 'one door West of the house of Col. Owen' two weeks earlier (1834-03-04, claim c008 there) — so court house and clerk's office are two buildings and not one. THE ATTACHED PROPERTY IS ALSO A BUILDING: 'a certain dwelling house and tenement' on a described quarter-quarter section, worth $759.50 against it. THE LEGAL DESCRIPTION IS DAMAGED and is NOT repaired: the transcription's township and range digits are broken ('town 4), north range 4 east'), so the normalized reading brackets what the surviving type will bear and asserts no location on the ground. Nothing here is placed on the plat.

claims.notes: LOOSE CATTLE, DESCRIBED EAR BY EAR, AND A COUNTY OFFICER'S ESTRAY BOOK BEHIND THEM. The estray machinery is one of the kinds of claim T-0258 asks for by name, and this is what it looks like in practice: four head taken up, each identified by its ear marks — crops, slits, forks, an upper slope — appraised at forty-eight dollars in front of a justice of the peace, and entered in the clerk's estray book, from which this is 'a true copy'. The ear marks matter because they are the town's system of ownership for animals that will not stay put, and because they say the beasts were RANGING: 1834 Chicago is a place where three-year-old cattle wander into somebody's lot and have to be advertised. THE OPENING LINES ARE LOST — the transcription's Vision reading failed and the head-line naming the taker-up's residence is bracketed uncertain — so the first animal's description is missing and is not supplied. Reynolds's own place is given only as 'living in Cook co.', not as Chicago, and is left at that. THE THIRD APPRAISER'S SURNAME IS NOT LEGIBLE and no person is minted for him.

claims.notes: THE SAME ADVERTISEMENT, FINALLY LEGIBLE — and it names a corner. On 1834-03-04 this notice sat in page 3 column 5 with its address crushed to 'the New Store on the coon of Legit' and could not be claimed; here the type reads clean: 'the New Store on the corner of South Water and Clark-streets'. That is why a month is read rather than an issue. KIMBALL IS THE SECOND DOCUMENTED OCCUPANT OF THAT CROSSING: the Chicago Democrat's own imprint gives the paper's office as 'corner of South Water and Clark[-]s[treets]' (1834-03-04, claim c032 there). Two occupants, one named corner, four possible quadrants, and nothing printed to choose between them — recorded, not resolved. W. Kimball is one of the ~24 findings the scan-verified record of Vol. I No. 1 enumerates, so his store is documented from November 1833 through March 1834 continuously.

claims.notes: A LOT AND A BLOCK, NAMED BY NUMBER — the only claim in the month that cites the plat directly. 'Block 120, in the School Section' is Section 16, the section reserved for schools in every township of the survey and sold off in Chicago from 1833; a block number that high places it well outside the original town plat, which runs to the eighties. THE LOT IS NOT PLACED ON THE GROUND HERE and no coordinate is derived from it: what is claimed is that this parcel was on the market in March 1834 through P. Pruyne & Co., and that the School Section was being sold in numbered blocks and lots by then. It is not the only such offer in the month — J. T. Temple advertises 'Eight Blocks for sale in the School Section' on 25 March (claim c007 there) — and together they show a land market a mile ahead of the built town.

claims.notes: THE TOWN'S WHOLE CONNECTION TO THE WORLD, IN FOUR LINES AND ONE DAY A WEEK. Chicago in March 1834 has four mails — eastern, western, northern, southern — and every one of them ARRIVES on Tuesday or Wednesday and DEPARTS Thursday morning at six, except the southern which leaves Saturday. So the post office is idle for four days and then handles the entire week's traffic in about thirty-six hours, which is also why the Democrat was published on Tuesdays: the paper is timed to the mail. The eight-o'clock departure for the east against six for the rest is the only variation and is recorded as printed. Signed by the postmaster, who is the same John S. C. Hogan who kept the store carried on from Brewster, Hogan & Co. — so the mail schedule and the counter are the same room.

claims.notes: WHAT IT COST TO BUILD IN CHICAGO IN MARCH 1834, PRINTED WEEKLY. The Prices Current carries a BUILDING MATERIALS block and it is the most directly useful table in the month for a reconstruction that has to reason about what a given owner could afford: assorted poplar lumber at twenty to twenty-three dollars the thousand feet, shingles at three to four, brick at six dollars the thousand, stone by the barrel at a dollar twenty-five. Read against them, the sidewalk ordinance of 4 March — gravel OR brick, the owner's choice — becomes a cost decision rather than a taste one. THE FIGURES ARE READ OFF A BROKEN TABLE AND SOME ARE NOT RECOVERABLE. The transcription has run the price column into the neighbouring text and lost several rows outright; 'Square timber, length' survives with no figure at all and is quoted with none supplied. Only the rows whose digits are legible are read, and the `lines_of_claim` name exactly those lines — nothing between them is smoothed into a number. THE REPORTER IS THE STOREKEEPER at the corner of LaSalle and South Water (1834-03-04, claim c012 there), which is worth knowing when weighing the table: these are one merchant's quotations, corrected weekly, and not a market return.

claims.notes: A WORKSHOP HIRING, WHICH IS EVIDENCE OF A TRADE'S SIZE. Reed wants two or three JOURNEYMEN cabinet makers at good wages — so his shop is bigger than one bench, and there is enough furniture work in a town of a few hundred to keep three trained men busy. He is the SECOND cabinet maker documented in the month, beside A. Filer & Co. who opened on South Water Street three doors north of the Baptist meeting house on 4 March, and there is a third in the same trade in the garrison: the deserter of 1834-03-25 is 'by occupation a cabinet maker' (claim c002 there). THE ADVERTISEMENT ENDS BADLY FOR HIM. On 25 March the whole of a cabinet shop's plant is auctioned 'at the shop of S. [W.] Reed' — three first-rate cabinet benches, a full set of tools, hardware and cherry lumber (claim c005 there) — so the shop that was hiring in December is being sold up by the end of March. The initials disagree between the two printings and are NOT reconciled here; both are recorded as printed and no merge is declared.

claims.notes: THE STORE THAT OTHER PEOPLE'S ADDRESSES ARE MEASURED FROM. Kinzie's own advertisement gives no address at all — only barrels and a date — but John Wellmaker's Man Trap is placed 'opposite Mr. R. A. Kinzie's Store' (1834-03-04, claim c031 there), so the store is a landmark the town navigated by even though its keeper never printed where it was. That asymmetry is worth recording, because it is how the anchors in this corpus mostly arise: a business becomes an address by being cited, not by advertising itself as one. NO PLACEMENT IS CLAIMED for Kinzie here; the associated place on his entity is the borrowed one and is worded as such. A second Kinzie — J. H. Kinzie — appears in these issues as a Chicago reference for a Buffalo mill-stone house, and no relation between the two is asserted.

claims.notes: A NAME THE CORPUS DID NOT HAVE. Haddock advertises fifty barrels of superfine flour and nothing else — no address, no trade description, no head-line — and he is recorded for exactly that reason: a reading pass that only extracted the placeable storefronts would leave the town under-populated with the merchants who took a two-line advertisement. RULING 3 puts him in the 1835 town under a survival liberty; NO PLACEMENT is claimed and none is inferred. Flour is the month's most-advertised commodity by some distance — Pruyne, Botsford, Kinzie, Haddock and Foot all sell it in these three issues — because the lake is shut and everything eaten in the town in March came in before the ice.

claims.notes: THE SAME TIMBER ADVERTISEMENT, READ OFF A BETTER CROP — and this is the printing that settles two things the 4 March one could not. THE AGENT'S NAME: 'J. ALLEN, Agent', where the earlier column read 'Many, ALLEN'. THE POPLAR SPECIFICATION: 'provided it be in logs [50] feet long, that will square 14 inches, throughout', where the earlier crop had lost the length entirely. Fifty-foot poplar logs squaring fourteen inches are the RAFT the oak was floated down on, so the harbour works consumed two grades of timber and only one of them ended up in the piers. It is claimed again rather than left as a duplicate because a reading pass's job is to record which witness carries which fact, and the two printings differ in what they will bear. The deadline stands unchanged: one third of the oak at the Piers by 15 April 1834.
